title: When I Am Afraid
sum: A man hunted by enemies who twist his words and watch his steps prays to God for help. Twice he stops and steadies himself with a refrain: "In God I praise his word. In God I have trusted, and I do not fear. What will flesh do to me?" God has counted his wanderings and kept his tears in a bottle. The psalm ends with the vow of a thank offering, sure that God will rescue him to walk "in the light of life".

The title links the psalm with David's flight to Gath (1 Samuel 21:10–15). It opens a run of five miktams (56–60) and a longer run of David psalms (51–65, 68–70) in the Elohistic Psalter, where "God" stands where other psalms say "the LORD". In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 55.

Witnesses for Psalms 56–72: the writer checked the Greek (Rahlfs) personally for Psalms 56, 58–60, 62, 63, 65, 66 and 68–72, and the contents of the Dead Sea Scrolls 4QPs-a and 11QPs-d in the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible (Abegg, Flint and Ulrich). DJD 16, the Syriac, the Targum (cited through Stec) and Jerome's Latin are cited as reported by others, not checked.

views.H: Read with its title, this is David's prayer in Gath, among the Philistines who knew him as Israel's hero, when he was "badly frightened of Achish" (1 Samuel 21:12). The fear and the trust both make sense there: a man alone in an enemy city, whose words could be twisted into a death sentence.
views.C: Form critics class Psalm 56 as an individual lament with a strong note of trust and a closing vow of thanks. The refrain (56:3–4, 10–11) marks its sections. Most date it to the time of the kings or later and treat the title as a reader's link with David's story, made by matching the psalm's fear and enemies to a scene in Samuel.
views.L: The refrain has become a prayer of its own for anyone who is afraid. The question of 56:11 returns in 118:6 and Hebrews 13:6. The tear bottle (56:8) has given comfort to many in grief.
views.J: The Midrash and the medieval commentators read the title's "silent dove far away" as Israel in exile, silent and scattered among the nations, and the psalm as the prayer of the people as well as of David. Rashi links the dove with David among the Philistines.
views.X: Augustine heard Christ and his church in every psalm: here the church far from home, mocked and watched, praising God's word. Calvin stressed the refrain as a model of faith fighting fear: trust does not remove fear at once, but answers it.

settings.what: A lament with a refrain of trust and a vow of thanks
settings.by: A hunted man; the title names David
settings.to: God, with the refrain spoken also to himself
settings.when: The title: when the Philistines seized David in Gath (1 Samuel 21:10–15). Scholars: any time of persecution by powerful enemies, perhaps a court case or plot
settings.why: To ask God to stop enemies who twist the singer's words and plot his death, and to steady his own fear by repeating what he knows: God keeps count of his tears and is on his side. The closing vow promises a thank offering at the sanctuary once he is rescued.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, singing and praying the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple and in their homes and gatherings. Under foreign rule they too lived among powerful neighbors, and the title invited them to pray as David did in Gath.
views: The title's setting: David's own prayer, alone and frightened in a Philistine city.
Many form critics: a prayer used at the sanctuary by someone falsely accused, with a vow to be paid later (compare 66:13–15).

title: In the Shadow of Your Wings
sum: Hiding from enemies who are like lions, the singer takes shelter "in the shadow of your wings" and calls on God Most High. A refrain, "Rise up high over the heavens, God! Your glory over all the earth!", closes each half. In the second half fear turns to song: his heart is firm, and he will wake the dawn with harp and lyre and thank God among the nations.

The title ties the psalm to David's hiding in a cave from Saul (1 Samuel 22:1; 24:3). Its second half (57:7–11) appears again as the first half of Psalm 108. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 56.

views.H: In the cave at Adullam or En-gedi, David hid with his men while Saul hunted him. In 1 Samuel 24 Saul walked into the very cave, and David spared him. Readers who follow the title hear in "they have fallen into the middle of it" (57:6) the trap that Saul himself walked into.
views.C: Most scholars see an individual lament that turns into a song of thanks, built in two halves with a refrain. The night-to-morning movement (57:4, 8) may reflect a night spent at the sanctuary waiting for God's answer at dawn. The reuse of 57:7–11 in Psalm 108 shows that its second half could stand on its own as a hymn.
views.L: "I will wake the dawn" made this a morning psalm. In the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it is sung at morning prayer (Lauds), and 57:7–11 is a favorite opening for worship.
views.J: The Talmud's story of David's lyre playing by itself at midnight and waking him before dawn (Berakhot 3b) grows from 57:8.
views.X: The church fathers read the refrain as a prophecy of Christ's resurrection and ascension: God "rising high over the heavens" in the risen Son, with his glory spreading to the nations through the gospel (57:9). Augustine heard Christ's prayer in the tomb in the first half and the risen Christ's praise in the second.

settings.what: A lament that becomes a dawn song of praise
settings.by: A singer surrounded by enemies; the title names David
settings.to: God; in 57:8, the singer's own soul and his instruments
settings.when: The title: when David fled from Saul into the cave (1 Samuel 22:1 or 1 Samuel 24:3). Scholars: perhaps a night of waiting at the sanctuary for God's answer, ending at dawn
settings.why: To seek shelter with God against enemies who are like lions, and then to praise him at daybreak among the nations. The refrain makes the rescue of one person a showing of God's glory to the world.
settings.readers: Later Israel: For them the refrain, "Your glory over all the earth!", was a hope for God's rule among the nations that held them.

title: Is There a God Who Judges?
sum: Psalm 58 is an attack on corrupt judges. It opens by asking "you gods", the rulers or heavenly powers who should give justice, whether they really do, and answers no: their hands "weigh out violence". The wicked are liars from birth, like a cobra that will not hear the charmer. Then come some of the harshest curses in the Psalms: broken teeth, draining water, a dissolving snail, a stillborn child, and the righteous washing their feet in blood.

The goal is stated at the end: that people will say, "Yes, a God exists who judges on the earth." Many Christians and Jews find the psalm hard to pray; the Roman Catholic Liturgy of the Hours leaves it out. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 57.
readings: Read as a cry for justice

The psalm is about public injustice: rulers who take bribes and shed blood. Its curses are the anger of the powerless, handed over to God rather than acted out. Seen this way, it is a protest that refuses to accept that might makes right, and its last line is a confession of faith that God will act.
Read as a judgment on the gods

If the "gods" are heavenly powers set over the nations (as in Psalm 82), the psalm imagines a heavenly court in which God condemns the rulers behind the world's injustice. Some scholars connect it with Deuteronomy 32:8 and Daniel 10:13.
Read as a prayer too hard to pray

Many readers, Jewish and Christian, have found the curses of 58:6–10 at odds with the command to love enemies. Some leave the psalm unread; others read it as Christ's judgment on evil, or as an honest model of bringing rage to God instead of acting on it.

views.H: Readers who take the title at face value think of David facing Saul's unjust courtiers, or of corrupt judges in his kingdom (2 Samuel 15:2–4). The "Do Not Destroy" tune ties it with Psalms 57 and 59.
views.C: Scholars class Psalm 58 as a community lament or a prophetic judgment speech, close to Psalm 82 and to the prophets' attacks on corrupt judges (Isaiah 1:23; Micah 3:9–11). Its many rare words make parts of 58:7–9 very uncertain.
views.L: The Roman Catholic Liturgy of the Hours omits Psalm 58 from its four-week cycle (with Psalms 83 and 109) because of its curses. The Orthodox and churches that sing the whole Psalter keep it. Churches that sing only psalms sing it with the rest.
views.J: Rashi applies the psalm to Saul's men, or to Saul's court where David was falsely accused. The Talmud reads "silence" (elem) in 58:1 as a lesson: one should be silent in this world, but "speak righteousness" in the study of Torah (Chullin 89a).
views.X: Augustine read the cobra that will not hear as those who refuse the gospel, and the washing of feet in blood as the righteous learning from God's judgment. Calvin defended the psalm as zeal for God's justice rather than personal hatred. C. S. Lewis called the hatred in such psalms wicked, yet valuable as a sign of how seriously Israel took wrong.

settings.what: An accusation against unjust rulers and a curse on the wicked
settings.by: A singer speaking for the victims of injustice; the title names David
settings.to: "You gods", the rulers or heavenly powers (58:1–2), and then God (58:6–9)
settings.when: No occasion is given. Scholars think of a time when courts and rulers were corrupt, as the prophets complain in the 700s BC, or of Judah under foreign rule
settings.why: To expose rulers who deal out violence instead of justice, to ask God to break their power, and to declare that a God who judges exists. Knowing that the targets are judges and rulers, not private rivals, changes how the curses read.
settings.readers: Later Israel, ruled by foreign governors and sometimes by unjust local leaders, who heard in it the promise that heaven had not given up on justice.
views: The "gods" are Israel's or the nations' judges and kings, given the title because they judge in God's place.
The "gods" are members of the divine council, as in Psalm 82, condemned for the injustice done under their rule.

title: Dogs Around the City
sum: Enemies prowl around the city every evening like growling dogs, their words like swords. The singer, innocent of any crime, calls on the LORD God of Armies to wake up and punish "all the nations". He asks God not to kill them at once, so that his people will not forget, but to make them stagger and then end them. A refrain, "My Strength", ends both halves: at first "I will watch for you", at the last "I will make music to you".
The title links it with the night Saul's men watched David's house and Michal let him down through a window (1 Samuel 19:11–17). In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 58.

views.H: Read with the title, the dogs are Saul's agents posted around David's house through the night. The prayer of "Do not kill them" then fits David's later refusal to kill Saul (1 Samuel 24; 26).
views.C: The references to "all the nations" (59:5, 8) suggest a king or a city surrounded by foreign enemies. Many scholars think a royal or national lament was later linked with David's story, or that an individual lament was widened for community use. The two halves each have a complaint about the dogs (59:6, 14) and a refrain (59:9, 17).
views.L: The psalm moves from evening, when the dogs prowl (59:6, 14), to morning, when the singer shouts for joy at God's loyal love (59:16). Christian readers have often prayed it as a prayer of the night watch, waiting for morning.
views.J: The Midrash reads the psalm with the story of Michal, and Rashi applies "the nations" to Saul's men, who behaved like foreigners toward David. Radak takes the psalm as David's prayer that also speaks for Israel among the nations.
views.X: Augustine applied 59:11, "Do not kill them", to the Jewish people, scattered but preserved as witnesses to the Scriptures (City of God 18.46). The reading shaped medieval Christian treatment of Jews for both protection and humiliation; modern Catholic and Protestant teaching has rejected it (compare Nostra Aetate 4).

settings.what: A lament against prowling enemies, with a refrain of trust
settings.by: A man under threat; the title names David
settings.to: God, whom the singer calls "my Strength"
settings.when: The title: when Saul sent men to watch David's house to kill him (1 Samuel 19:11). Scholars: perhaps a king or city surrounded by foreign enemies
settings.why: To ask God to rescue the innocent singer, to show the nations that God rules "in Jacob to the ends of the earth", and to bring the enemies down slowly enough that God's people remember it.
settings.readers: Later Israel: The prowling dogs of the nations around Jerusalem (compare Nehemiah 4:7–8) gave the psalm a new setting.
views: The title's setting: one man's prayer at night in a watched house.
Many scholars: a king's or community's prayer against foreign enemies, perhaps in the 700s BC or after the exile.

title: You Have Rejected Us
sum: Israel has been beaten in battle, and the psalm says God himself has thrown them off: he has shaken the land and made his people drink a wine that makes them reel. In the middle comes God's answer from his holy place: all the tribes are his, and the neighboring nations, Moab, Edom and Philistia, are his servants. The psalm ends with the question who will lead the army to Edom, and the confidence that "with God we will do mighty things".
The title connects it with David's wars against Aram and Edom (2 Samuel 8; 10). Its second half (60:5–12) appears again in Psalm 108. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 59.

views.H: Following the title, the psalm was written while David was fighting in the north against Aram, when Edom attacked from the south and the land seemed lost. Joab's victory in the Valley of Salt followed. The title's "twelve thousand" differs from the eighteen thousand of 2 Samuel 8:13 and 1 Chronicles 18:12.
views.C: Most scholars see a community lament after a defeat, with an oracle of God in the middle (60:6–8). The oracle may be older than the lament around it. Dates proposed range from David's time to the exile, when Edom took Judah's land (Obadiah 10–14).
views.L: The psalm became a prayer for nations at war and in defeat. Its last two verses, "rescue by human beings is empty" and "With God we will do mighty things", are often prayed in times of national crisis.
views.J: Rashi reads the title with 2 Samuel 8 and the oracle as God's promise of the whole land. The medieval commentators read "Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine" as a claim to the land east of the Jordan as well as the west.
views.X: The church fathers read the oracle of 60:6–8 as Christ's victory over the nations: the dividing of Shechem and Succoth as the gospel going out to all, and the sandal over Edom as the humbling of pride. Calvin read the psalm as a lesson in national humility before God.

settings.what: A community lament after defeat, with an oracle of God
settings.by: The king or a leader speaking for the defeated people ("us", "me"); the title names David; the oracle is God's own speech
settings.to: God; the oracle (60:6–8) is spoken by God, perhaps through a temple prophet, to the people
settings.when: The title: during David's wars with Aram-naharaim, Aram-zobah and Edom. Scholars: after a defeat, often thought to be by Edom
settings.why: To bring a military disaster before God, to hear his claim that the land and the nations are still his, and to renew trust that the army can win only with God. The title's word "for teaching" says it was to be learned.
settings.readers: Later Israel, who had lost their land to Babylon and watched Edomites settle in southern Judah, and heard God's oracle as a promise that the land was still his.
views: The title: written in the crisis of David's war on two fronts.
Some scholars: a lament of the exile, when Edom took Judah's southern land.

title: The Rock Higher Than I
sum: From "the edge of the earth", far away and faint, the singer asks God to lead him to a rock too high to climb alone, and to let him live as a guest in God's tent under the cover of his wings. Then the prayer turns to the king: long life, a throne before God forever, guarded by loyal love and faithfulness. It ends with a promise to sing and keep vows every day.
It is one of the shortest psalms in Book II. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 60.

views.H: Readers of the title think of David far from Jerusalem, perhaps during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15–17) east of the Jordan, longing for the tent where the ark was kept, and praying for his own reign.
views.C: Scholars class it as an individual lament with a royal prayer (61:6–7). The speaker may be the king himself, or a worshiper whose prayer was joined to a prayer for the king. The "tent" and "wings" point to the sanctuary.
views.L: "Lead me onto a rock that is too high for me" has been taken into many hymns. Many churches use it as a prayer for those far from home.
views.J: The Targum renders 61:6–7 as a prayer for "King Messiah", whose years will last for generations. Rashi reads "the edge of the earth" as the exile, and the psalm as Israel's prayer from the lands of the dispersion.
views.X: Christian readers heard the king of 61:6–7 as Christ, whose reign has no end, and the rock as Christ himself (1 Corinthians 10:4). Augustine heard the church praying "from the end of the earth", from every nation.

settings.what: A prayer from far away, with a prayer for the king
settings.by: A singer far from the sanctuary; the title names David
settings.to: God
settings.when: No occasion is given. Readers of the title think of David in exile from Jerusalem; scholars of a king at war or a worshiper far from the temple
settings.why: To ask to be brought to safety and to the sanctuary, and to pray for the king's long reign under God's protection. The two parts join the safety of one person with the safety of the king's rule.
settings.readers: Later Israel, praying "from the end of the earth" for themselves and for the Davidic king they hoped would come.

title: Quiet Before God
sum: Psalm 62 is a psalm of trust with almost no request in it. Six of its lines open with the same small Hebrew word, akh, "yes, only": only God is the singer's rock, only in him is rest. Enemies batter him like a leaning wall, blessing with their mouths and cursing inside. He turns to the people and tells them to trust God and pour out their hearts, because human beings, high or low, weigh less than a breath on the scales, and wealth is no place to rest a heart.

It ends with a saying heard "once" and "two times": strength belongs to God, and so does loyal love, for he pays each person back by what he does. The title names Jeduthun, one of David's chief musicians. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 61.

views.H: Those who follow the title think of David in a time of betrayal at court, perhaps Absalom's plot, when trusted men flattered him and schemed against him (2 Samuel 15:1–12). Jeduthun led one of the temple guilds of singers (1 Chronicles 16:41–42; 25:1–6).
views.C: Scholars call it a psalm of trust. It moves from the singer's own calm (62:1–7) to teaching the congregation (62:8–12), in the manner of wisdom teaching. The number saying in 62:11 ("once ... two times") is a wisdom form also found in Proverbs 30 and Job 33:14.
views.L: "My soul is quiet before God" has made the psalm a favorite for silent prayer and for retreats. Many Christian contemplative writers take 62:1 and 62:5 as a call to wordless trust, and the Taizé community has set its opening as a chant.
views.J: Rashi reads Jeduthun as a reference to the "decrees" (datot) laid on Israel, and the psalm as Israel's patience under them. Jewish commentators read the closing pair, strength and loyal love, as God's two qualities of justice and mercy (din and rachamim) working together.
views.X: Paul's statement that God "will pay back each person according to his works" (Romans 2:6) echoes 62:12, along with Proverbs 24:12, and Jesus says the same in Matthew 16:27. Christian interpreters have used the verse in debates about grace and works: Catholic writers to show that God rewards good works, Protestant writers to show that judgment is by works even though justification is by faith.

echoes: 1 Chronicles 25:1–6; 39:0; 77:0; 39:5–6; 49:6–7; Proverbs 24:12; Romans 2:6; Matthew 16:27; Revelation 22:12; Job 33:14

settings.what: A psalm of trust that becomes teaching
settings.by: A singer under attack from false friends; the title names David
settings.to: His own soul (62:5), his attackers (62:3–4), then the people (62:8–10), and finally God (62:12)
settings.when: No occasion is given. Some think of David's court during Absalom's plot; many scholars of any time of social conflict, when the rich and powerful seemed safe
settings.why: To teach the congregation, from the singer's own experience, that rest is found only in God, that people and money cannot be trusted, and that God both rules and loves.
settings.readers: Later Israel, who lived under powerful patrons and governors and needed the reminder that the great "weigh less than a breath".

title: Thirsty for God
sum: In a dry land without water the singer says his soul is thirsty for God and his body aches for him. He remembers seeing God's strength and glory in the holy place, and he says God's loyal love is better than life itself. At night on his bed he thinks about God and sings in the shadow of his wings, clinging close behind him. The enemies will go down to the depths, and the king will rejoice in God.
The title places it "in the wilderness of Judah", where David hid from Saul and later fled from Absalom. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 62.

views.H: David fled into the Judean wilderness twice: hunted by Saul (1 Samuel 23:14–15; 24:1) and when Absalom rebelled (2 Samuel 15:23–28; 16:2, 14). Since the psalm speaks of "the king" (63:11), many readers think of the flight from Absalom, when David crossed the Kidron toward the wilderness and sent the ark back to Jerusalem.
views.C: Scholars call it an individual psalm of trust, perhaps from a king or worshiper kept away from the temple, or from someone who has spent a night at the sanctuary seeking God (63:2, 6). The image of thirst for God is shared with 42:1–2 and 143:6.
views.L: Psalm 63 has been a morning psalm since the early church. John Chrysostom said that the fathers ordered it sung every morning. It is the first psalm of Sunday morning prayer in the Roman Liturgy of the Hours, and it is one of the Six Psalms read at the start of Orthodox Matins.
views.J: Jewish interpreters read the wilderness of Judah as Israel's exile, and the longing to see God "in the holy place" as the longing for the rebuilt temple. Rashi takes "the king" in 63:11 as David himself.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in 63:1 the soul's thirst for God that only Christ satisfies (John 4:13–14; 7:37). Augustine read 63:8, "My soul clings close behind you", as the glue of love that holds the soul to God.

settings.what: A psalm of longing and trust
settings.by: A worshiper far from the sanctuary, perhaps a king; the title names David
settings.to: God, and in 63:11 about the king
settings.when: The title: "when he was in the wilderness of Judah". Scholars: a king or worshiper away from the temple, or keeping a night watch in it
settings.why: To put into words a longing for God himself, more than for his gifts, and to trust that those who seek the singer's life will fail. It was kept as a prayer of desire for God.
settings.readers: Later Israel: Those who lived far from Jerusalem, in Babylon or Egypt, sang of longing to see God in his holy place.
views: David hid in the Judean wilderness before he was king (1 Samuel 23–24).
David as king fled into the wilderness, which fits "the king" in 63:11 (2 Samuel 15–17).

title: The Arrow of God
sum: Psalm 64 is a short lament against plotters. They sharpen their tongues like swords and shoot bitter words like arrows from hiding, sure that no one will see. Then God shoots them with his own arrow, their own tongues trip them up, and all who see them shake their heads. The psalm ends with the righteous glad in the LORD.
The main weapon in it is speech: slander, plotting and secret talk. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 63.

views.H: Readers of the title think of the plots against David at Saul's court or during Absalom's revolt, when Ahithophel's counsel was turned against him (2 Samuel 15:31; 17:14).
views.C: Scholars classify it as an individual lament against enemies who use words as weapons, perhaps false accusers or people using curses. The reversal is exact: those who shoot "suddenly" (64:4) are shot "suddenly" (64:7).
views.L: The psalm is used in many churches as a prayer against slander and gossip.
views.J: Rashi applies it to Daniel's enemies in the lions' den, who plotted against him in secret (Daniel 6), following the Midrash, which reads this psalm with that story.
views.X: Augustine read Psalm 64 as the passion of Christ: the plotters as the leaders who planned his death in secret, and God's arrow as the judgment that fell on Jerusalem. Calvin read it as a comfort for any believer slandered by the powerful.

settings.what: A lament against slanderers
settings.by: A man targeted by plotters; the title names David
settings.to: God
settings.when: No occasion is given. Scholars think of a false accusation or a plot, perhaps at court or in the town gate
settings.why: To ask protection from enemies who use words to destroy, and to trust that God will turn their own words against them so that everyone learns from it.
settings.readers: Later Israel, where rumor and accusation against the community were common (Ezra 4:6–16).

title: The Crowned Year
sum: Psalm 65 is a hymn of thanks for rain and harvest. It opens in Zion, where prayer is heard, vows are paid and sins are atoned for. Then it widens to the whole world: God set the mountains firm and calms the seas and the uproar of the peoples. Last comes the farm: God visits the land and waters it, softens the furrows with showers, and crowns the year so that the hills and meadows are wrapped in flocks and grain and seem to shout and sing.
In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 64. The Greek title adds "a song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, from the account of the exile, when they were about to go out" (see the variant at 65:0).

views.H: Readers of the title link it with David, perhaps after the end of the three-year famine (2 Samuel 21:1, 14), when God answered prayer for the land.
views.C: Scholars call it a community hymn of thanks, most likely for a festival. Some think of the autumn feast of Booths, when the year turned and the rains were awaited; others of the spring barley harvest. The three scenes (temple, cosmos, fields) show God as forgiver, creator and giver of rain.
views.L: Psalm 65 is a standard harvest-festival psalm in Protestant churches and is read at Rogation and Thanksgiving services.
views.J: The Talmud and Midrash read 65:1, "silence is praise", as a lesson that the highest praise of God is silence, since no words are enough (Megillah 18a).
views.X: Augustine read the psalm as the song of the exiles longing for Jerusalem, using the Greek title. Christian writers have used 65:2, "all flesh will come to you", for the gathering of the nations to Christ, and 65:9–13 in teaching on God's providence.

settings.what: A festival hymn of thanks for forgiveness, creation and harvest
settings.by: A temple singer leading the congregation ("we", 65:3–5); the title names David
settings.to: God
settings.when: No occasion is given. Scholars think of a harvest feast, perhaps Booths in the autumn, or a service after rain had ended a drought
settings.why: To thank God for answered prayer, forgiven sin and a good year, and to see the same God at work in the temple, in the cosmos and in the fields.
settings.readers: Later Israel, farmers in a small province who knew that a failed rain meant hunger (Haggai 1:10–11).

title: Come and See
sum: Psalm 66 begins by calling the whole earth to shout to God and remember the crossing of the sea and the river. Israel has been tested like silver in the fire, caught in a net and run over, but brought out to plenty. Then one voice takes over: the singer comes to the temple with burnt offerings to pay the vows he made in trouble, and tells those who fear God what God has done for him.
The psalm moves from the nations, to the people, to one person. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 65, and the Greek title adds "of resurrection".

views.H: There is no named author. Some readers link it with Hezekiah's rescue from Assyria (2 Kings 19) and his thanksgiving after illness (Isaiah 38:20), where a king's rescue and the nation's coincide.
views.C: Scholars see two parts: a community hymn (66:1–12) and an individual thanksgiving with sacrifice (66:13–20). Some think a king offered thanks for the nation; others that two pieces were joined for use in the temple. The crossing of the sea and the river (66:6) joins the Exodus and the crossing of the Jordan (Joshua 3).
views.L: "Come and see" and "Come and listen" made it a psalm of testimony in Christian worship. The Greek title "of resurrection" led early Christian readers to hear it as an Easter psalm, and the Roman rite still sings it in the Easter season.
views.J: Jewish interpreters read "through the fire and the water" as Israel's trials in every exile, with Isaiah 43:2.
views.X: The church fathers read the psalm, with its Greek title, as a song of Christ's resurrection and of baptism (passing through the water). Christian teachers have used 66:18 to warn that cherished sin hinders prayer.

echoes: Exodus 14:21–22; Joshua 3:14–17; Isaiah 43:2; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:3; 1 Peter 1:7; 22:25; 116:14; Genesis 28:20–22

settings.what: A hymn calling the earth to praise God for his rescue of Israel
settings.by: A leader of worship
settings.to: All the earth and the peoples, and God
settings.when: No occasion is given. Scholars think of a temple festival after a national rescue
settings.why: To call the world to praise God for the Exodus and for bringing his people through testing to plenty.
settings.readers: Later Israel, who had been through "fire and water" in the exile and found in the psalm the pattern of testing and rescue.

settings.what: A thanksgiving with sacrifice and a public testimony
settings.by: One worshiper, perhaps a king
settings.to: God (66:13–15), then those who fear God (66:16–20)
settings.when: The time of paying vows at the temple after rescue
settings.why: To keep vows made in trouble and to tell others what God did, so that thanks becomes testimony.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile bringing their own thank offerings and vows to the rebuilt temple (Ezra 6:16–17).

title: Let All the Peoples Thank You
sum: Psalm 67 takes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24–26, "May the LORD make his face shine toward you", and asks that its result be that the whole earth will know God's way. Twice comes the refrain "Let the peoples thank you, God; let the peoples thank you, all of them." In the center the nations rejoice because God judges them fairly. At the end the land has given its crops, and the blessing on Israel becomes a reason for all the ends of the earth to fear God.
It is a short psalm, perhaps sung at a harvest. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 66.

views.H: The psalm has no named author and no stated occasion. Its harvest line (67:6) and use of the priestly blessing point to a festival at the temple.
views.C: Scholars see a harvest prayer or blessing, built in a careful symmetry around the central verse 67:4. Some call it a missionary psalm: Israel is blessed so that the nations will come to know God, as in God's promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3).
views.L: In the Book of Common Prayer (1662) Psalm 67, Deus misereatur, is the alternative to the Song of Simeon at Evening Prayer. Many churches sing it as a mission hymn and at harvest services.
views.J: Psalm 67 is recited in many Jewish communities during the counting of the Omer between Passover and Shavuot, because its seven verses (after the title) and forty-nine words (in the Hebrew after the title) match the seven weeks and forty-nine days. It is often printed in the shape of the seven-branched lampstand.
views.X: Christian readers have heard the shining face of God (67:1) in Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), and the call to the nations as the mission of the church (Luke 24:47). Augustine stressed that the blessing ends with "all the ends of the earth", not with Israel alone.

echoes: Numbers 6:24–26; Genesis 12:3; Leviticus 26:4; 98:2–3; 117:1; Isaiah 49:6; 2 Corinthians 4:6; Luke 2:30–32

settings.what: A prayer for blessing so that the nations may know God
settings.by: The congregation ("us"), led by a priest or singer
settings.to: God, and about the peoples
settings.when: No occasion is given. Scholars think of a harvest festival, when the priestly blessing was given
settings.why: To ask for God's blessing on Israel, not only for Israel's sake but so that all nations will come to praise him.
settings.readers: Later Israel, a small people among the nations, who sang that their blessing was meant to reach the ends of the earth.

title: God Marches from Sinai to Zion
sum: Psalm 68 is the hardest psalm in the Psalter to translate, and one of the most exciting to read. It opens with the words Moses said when the ark set out (Numbers 10:35), "Let God rise up! Let his enemies scatter", and then follows God on the march: from Sinai through the wilderness, where the earth shook and the skies dripped; through the conquest of Canaan, where kings ran away and women divided the plunder; to Zion, the mountain God chose over the high peaks of Bashan. He goes up on high with captives in his train. A procession of singers, musicians and girls with tambourines leads him into the holy place, with the tribes behind. Finally the kings of the earth, Egypt and Cush, are summoned to sing to the rider through the ancient heavens.

Much of the Hebrew is rare or obscure, and some lines (68:13, 68:30) may never be understood with certainty. Paul quotes 68:18 in Ephesians 4:8 in a form that says "gave" rather than "took". In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 67.
readings: Read as a festival procession

Most scholars think the psalm accompanied a procession bringing the ark, or a symbol of God's presence, up to the temple (68:24–27). Its scenes retell the story from Sinai to Zion so that the worshipers march with God into his house.
Read as a collection of song openings

W. F. Albright proposed that the psalm is a list of the first lines of some thirty older poems, which would explain its sudden jumps. Few scholars follow him fully, but many agree that it uses very old poetry, close to the Song of Deborah (Judges 5).
Read as Christ's ascension

Following Ephesians 4:8–10, Christians have read 68:18 as Christ going up to heaven after his victory over death and giving gifts to his church. The Eastern church sings its first verses at Easter, and Western churches read it at the Ascension and Pentecost.
Read as the giving of the Torah

The Targum and the Talmud read 68:18 as Moses going up Sinai to receive the Torah and bringing it down as a gift for Israel. Many Jewish communities read the psalm on Shavuot, the feast of the giving of the Torah.

views.H: Read with the title, David composed it for the bringing of the ark to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:12–19; 1 Chronicles 15–16), and 68:1 recalls the ark's journeys in the wilderness. The list of tribes in 68:27, with Benjamin first and Judah next, fits an early time when Benjamin, Saul's tribe, still had a leading place.
views.C: Scholars date the psalm anywhere from the time of the judges to after the exile. The old forms, the likeness to Judges 5 and Deuteronomy 33, and the northern tribes in 68:27 suggest very early material, reworked for Jerusalem. The images of God riding on the clouds (68:4, 33) and of a divine mountain match Canaanite poems about Baal, here claimed for Israel's God.
views.L: The Orthodox Church sings 68:1–3 again and again in the services of Pascha (Easter), with "Christ is risen". In the West it has been used at the Ascension and at Pentecost because of 68:18. Its opening has also been a battle hymn: the French Huguenots called it their "psalm of battles".
views.J: The Talmud (Shabbat 88b) reads 68:18 of Moses: when he went up on high to receive the Torah, the angels objected, and God told Moses to answer them. The Targum renders the verse as Moses going up to the heavens, learning the words of the Torah and giving them as gifts to people.
views.X: Ephesians 4:8 quotes 68:18 with "he gave gifts to people" and applies it to Christ, who went up after first going down "into the lower parts of the earth" (Ephesians 4:9). Christians have long debated what that descent was. Ethiopian Christians have treasured 68:31, "Cush will run to stretch out its hands to God", as a promise about their own land, and in the 1800s and 1900s many African and African American Christians took it as a sign of hope for Africa.

echoes: Numbers 10:35; Judges 5:4–5; Deuteronomy 33:2; Exodus 19:16–18; 2 Samuel 6:12–19; 1 Chronicles 15:16–28; Ephesians 4:8–10; Habakkuk 3:3–6; 18:7–15; 132:8; Zephaniah 3:10

settings.what: A victory hymn for a procession of God to his sanctuary
settings.by: A singer or choir leading a festival procession; the title names David
settings.to: God, the congregation, the mountains (68:16), the kingdoms of the earth (68:32)
settings.when: The title gives none. Traditional readers: the bringing of the ark to Jerusalem. Scholars: an autumn or spring festival procession, possibly using very old poems
settings.why: To celebrate God as the warrior who marched from Sinai, cared for orphans and widows, took the land, chose Zion and will be honored by all nations. Singing it made the worshipers part of his march into the holy place.
settings.readers: Later Israel: They had seen no kings bring gifts to Jerusalem, and the psalm's call to Egypt and Cush became a hope for the future.
views: The traditional setting: David's procession with the ark (2 Samuel 6).
Many scholars: a yearly procession celebrating God's kingship.
Albright and others: a set of very old song fragments joined for worship.

traditions.q: Paul reads Psalm 68:18 of Christ, who first "came down into the lower parts of the earth" (Ephesians 4:9). Do those words mean the incarnation, the grave or Hades? (Compare the card at Psalm 16:10.)
views: Christ went down to the realm of the dead after his death, not to free the damned but to free the righteous who had gone before him; this is the descent into hell of the Creed (Catechism 631–637).
Christ went down into Hades and broke its gates, raising Adam and Eve and the righteous, as the Easter icon of the Resurrection shows.
The whole person of Christ, after his burial, went down to hell to defeat the devil and proclaim his victory, not to suffer (Formula of Concord, article 9).
Many Reformed writers read Ephesians 4:9 as Christ's coming down to earth in the incarnation, or as his burial. Calvin read the Creed's descent as Christ's suffering of God's judgment on the cross.
Many Baptists read the lower parts of the earth as the earth itself, so the verse speaks of the incarnation; others take it of the grave. Most Baptist confessions do not mention a descent.

deep.h: Took gifts or gave gifts? (68:18 and Ephesians 4:8)
deep.b:
The Hebrew of 68:18 says God "took gifts among humans": a victorious king receiving tribute, or captives given as servants for his sanctuary (compare Numbers 8:16–19). The Greek translation keeps "you took". But Ephesians 4:8 has "he gave gifts to people", and so do the Aramaic Targum and the Syriac.

The likely explanation is that Paul followed a reading already known among Jews of his time, the one the Targum later preserved: Moses went up and gave the Torah as a gift. Paul applies the same pattern to Christ, who went up and gave gifts of apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers (Ephesians 4:11). Some interpreters add that a king who receives tribute also hands it out, so "took" and "gave" are two sides of one victory.

Jewish readers point out that the Targum's Moses reading and Paul's Christ reading use the same verse in opposite directions: one for the Torah given at Sinai, the other for the Spirit's gifts after the ascension. Christian readers have often linked them: Pentecost (Acts 2), fifty days after Easter, falls on Shavuot, the feast that later Judaism connected with the giving of the Torah.

deep.h: Why the psalm is so hard
deep.b:
Psalm 68 has more words that occur only once in the Bible than almost any other passage. Line 68:13 ("Even if you lie down between the saddlebags") and line 68:30 ("the herd of bulls among the calves of the peoples") are among the most uncertain in the Old Testament; the Plain gives the most likely sense and the notes give the alternatives. Some scholars think the psalm's sudden changes come from its use in a procession, where each section accompanied a stage; others think old poems were joined.

What is clear is the story: God marches from Sinai (68:7–8, close to Judges 5:4–5), gives the land (68:9–14), chooses Zion over Bashan (68:15–18), defeats his enemies (68:19–23), enters his sanctuary in procession (68:24–27), and receives the homage of the nations (68:28–35).

title: Water Up to the Throat
sum: Psalm 69 is a long lament from someone sinking in deep water and mud, worn out from calling to God. He is hated for no reason by more enemies than the hairs on his head. He admits his own foolishness, but most of his suffering is for God's sake: "Zeal for your house has eaten me up", and the insults aimed at God have landed on him. His own family treats him as a stranger, the drinkers make songs about him, and when he is thirsty they give him vinegar. Then the prayer turns into some of the strongest curses in the Psalms: let their table become a trap, their eyes go dark, their camp be ruined, and their names be wiped out of the scroll of life. It ends in praise and in a promise that God will rebuild the towns of Judah.
Psalm 69 is one of the psalms the New Testament quotes most, almost always of Jesus' suffering. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 68.
readings: Read as the prayer of a suffering righteous person

The speaker is a faithful Israelite mocked and shut out because of his zeal for God's house, perhaps during a time when the temple lay in ruins or was neglected (69:9, 35). His curses are the cry of a victim who has no one else to turn to (69:20).
Read as Christ's prayer

The New Testament hears Jesus speaking here: the zeal for God's house (John 2:17), hatred without cause (John 15:25), the insults borne for God (Romans 15:3), and the vinegar at the cross (Matthew 27:34, 48; John 19:28–29). Many Christians read the whole psalm as the Passion in prayer.
Read as Israel's prayer

Jewish interpreters such as Rashi read the waters as the nations and the speaker as Israel in exile, mocked for keeping faith with God, whose hope is the rebuilding of Zion and the cities of Judah (69:35).
Read as a curse psalm

Readers in every tradition have asked how 69:22–28 can be prayed. Some leave the verses out; some pray them as the words of Christ against evil, or as God's own judgment; others pray them honestly as an outcry of pain handed over to God (see the card on the curse psalms at Psalm 35).

views.H: Read with the title, David speaks of the scorn he faced for his zeal to build God's house (2 Samuel 7:2; 1 Chronicles 22:5–14), perhaps during Absalom's revolt, when his own family turned against him. Many traditional readers note that 69:35–36, on rebuilding the towns of Judah, fits a later time better.
views.C: Scholars call Psalm 69 an individual lament. Many date it to the exile or after, when Judah's towns lay in ruins and Jerusalem's temple was in ruins or newly rebuilt (69:9, 35–36). Some link the speaker with Jeremiah, who was mocked, thrown into a muddy pit (Jeremiah 38:6) and shut out by his family (Jeremiah 12:6).
views.L: In the old Holy Week night services (Tenebrae), Psalm 69 was sung on Maundy Thursday, and 69:20 is the text of the Palm Sunday offertory chant. In Judaism, 69:13 is said in the Sabbath afternoon service before the Torah reading.
views.J: Rashi and others read the psalm as Israel in exile. Jewish teachers have answered the Christian reading by pointing to 69:5: the speaker confesses his own foolishness and guilt, which they say cannot fit a sinless messiah. Jewish worship uses the prayer of 69:13, not the curses.
views.X: The New Testament quotes or echoes Psalm 69 at least a dozen times. Augustine answered the problem of 69:5 by saying that Christ speaks here in the person of his body, the church, or of the sins laid on him. Calvin read the curses as the prophetic voice of the Spirit against those who reject God, not as personal revenge. Many modern Christians pray the lament and leave the curses to God.

echoes: John 2:17; John 15:25; 35:19; Romans 15:3; Matthew 27:34; Matthew 27:48; John 19:28–29; Romans 11:9–10; Acts 1:20; 109:8; Revelation 3:5; Revelation 16:1; Jeremiah 38:6; Jeremiah 12:6; 40:2; 22:18

settings.what: An individual lament of one who suffers for God's sake
settings.by: A faithful Israelite mocked by many; the title names David
settings.to: God
settings.when: No occasion is given. Traditional readers: David. Scholars: a zealous worshiper in the exile or after, when the temple was in ruins or newly rebuilt; some suggest Jeremiah
settings.why: To lay before God a suffering that is unjust and caused by loyalty to God, and to ask God to act so that others who hope in him will not be ashamed (69:6).
settings.readers: Later Israel: Those who held to God's house when it was poor and mocked (Haggai 1:2–9; Nehemiah 4:1–5) found their own story in it.
views: The title: David mocked for his zeal for God's house.
Jeremiah or a prophet like him
Mocked, sunk in mud, cut off by family (Jeremiah 38:6; 12:6).
A worshiper zealous for the rebuilding of the temple and Judah (69:35).

settings.what: Curses on the enemies, then a vow of praise and a promise for Zion
settings.by: The same speaker
settings.to: God (69:22–29), then the humble (69:32) and all creation (69:34)
settings.when: The same occasion
settings.why: To hand the enemies over to God's judgment instead of taking revenge, and then to promise thanks that God will like better than an ox. The last lines widen one person's rescue into the rebuilding of Zion.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, for whom 69:35–36 promised the resettling of Judah, and who heard the curses as a plea against those who hated Zion.

traditions.q: Paul applies the curse of Psalm 69:22–23 to Israel's present hardening (Romans 11:9–10). How should that use be read?
views: The hardening is partial and temporary; the Jews are not rejected or accursed by God, and the church rejects any reading that blames the Jewish people as such for Christ's death (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597, 674, 839).

God has hardened part of Israel for a time so that the gentiles come in. Calvin read "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:26) of the whole people of God, Jews and gentiles; many later Reformed and Puritan writers expected a large turning of the Jewish people to Christ before the end.
The hardening belongs to the present church age; afterward God will turn again to national Israel, and the promises to it will be kept to the letter.
Luther's late writings used such texts harshly against the Jews. Modern Lutheran churches have publicly rejected those writings and read Romans 11 as Paul does, with hope for Israel.

traditions.q: "Let them be wiped out of the scroll of life" (69:28). Can a person's name be removed from the book of life?
views: The names of the elect are written from before creation and cannot be removed. The verse speaks of those who only seemed to belong, or of the scroll of the living on earth (Westminster Confession 17).
Most Baptists hold that a true believer cannot finally fall away, and read the verse as about the wicked who were never truly God's people (Second London Confession 17).
A true believer can turn away and be lost, so a name written in the book can be blotted out, as Exodus 32:33 and Revelation 3:5 suggest; John Wesley argued this from such texts.
No one can be sure of final perseverance without special revelation; grace can be lost through mortal sin and regained through repentance (Council of Trent, session 6).
The elect are kept by God, yet believers can fall from grace through unbelief; Lutherans hold both without a system to join them (Formula of Concord, article 11).

deep.b:
Psalm 69 is one of the psalms the New Testament uses most:

69:4, hated without reason: Jesus in John 15:25 (or 35:19). 69:9a, zeal for God's house: the disciples after the cleansing of the temple (John 2:17). 69:9b, insults aimed at God fall on the speaker: Paul of Christ (Romans 15:3). 69:21, poison (or gall) and vinegar: the wine mixed with gall and the sour wine at the cross (Matthew 27:34, 48; Mark 15:36; John 19:28–29). 69:22–23, the table as a trap and darkened eyes: Paul of Israel's present hardening (Romans 11:9–10), followed at once by his hope that it is not final (Romans 11:11). 69:25, a deserted camp: Peter of Judas (Acts 1:20, with Psalm 109:8). 69:24 and 69:28 stand behind the bowls of wrath and the book of life in Revelation (Revelation 16:1; 3:5).

The pattern is that the lament is applied to Jesus and the curses to those who oppose him. The New Testament does not make Jesus speak the curses; it reports them as fulfilled. Jesus' own words from the cross were a prayer for his enemies (Luke 23:34).

The curses ask that the enemies' meals become traps, their sight fail, their bodies shake, God's anger catch them, their camp be empty, guilt pile on guilt, and their names be wiped out of the scroll of life. They are not polite, and the Plain does not soften them.

Several things are worth weighing. The speaker asks God to act, and does not take revenge himself (compare Romans 12:19). The enemies are those who "hunt down the one you have struck" (69:26), kicking someone already down. The curses are a measure for measure: those who poisoned his food lose their table, those who mocked lose their tents. And the psalm goes straight on to praise and to hope for Zion.

Traditions differ on how to use them in worship (see the card at Psalm 35 and the topic page on the curse psalms). Erich Zenger argued that such psalms give the victims of violence words, and hand vengeance over to God so that the cycle of violence can stop. C. S. Lewis found the hatred in them wicked, but saw in it a sign that Israel took evil seriously, as people who do not care about right and wrong never would.

title: Hurry, God
sum: Psalm 70 is a five-verse cry for quick help: "God, to rescue me! LORD, hurry to my help!" It asks that those who want the singer's harm be turned back in shame, and that all who seek God rejoice and say at all times, "Great is God!" It ends where it began: "As for me, I am poor and needy; God, hurry to me!"

Psalm 70 is almost the same as 40:13–17, with small changes, most of them "God" where Psalm 40 has "the LORD", as in the rest of the Elohistic Psalter. The Plain uses the wording of 40:13–17 wherever the Hebrew is the same. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 69.

views.H: Read with its title, David wrote it "to bring to remembrance", as with Psalm 38, perhaps to accompany the memorial part of an offering (Leviticus 2:2) or to remind God of his need. Traditional readers take Psalm 40's closing section to have been reused by David himself as a short separate prayer.
views.C: Scholars debate which came first. Most think the short prayer was lifted out of Psalm 40 and edited for the Elohistic collection; some think Psalm 70 was an independent prayer that the author of Psalm 40 joined to his thanksgiving. Its placement here pairs it with Psalm 71, which continues its words (71:1–3, 12–13), and some Hebrew manuscripts join the two.
views.L: The opening verse has been the most used single line of the Psalter in Christian prayer. John Cassian taught it as a prayer to say at all times (Conferences 10.10), and in Latin, Deus in adiutorium meum intende; Domine ad adiuvandum me festina, it opens every hour of the Western daily office except the first of the day, which begins with 51:15. The Book of Common Prayer's "O God, make speed to save us; O Lord, make haste to help us" comes from it.
views.J: Jewish commentators read "to bring to remembrance" as a prayer that God remember his people's distress, as in the title of Psalm 38, and read the psalm as Israel's plea in trouble.
views.X: Cassian said the verse fits every need: temptation, fear, joy, weakness, and the fight against pride. Christian readers have heard in its last line, "I am poor and needy", the voice of Christ in his poverty (2 Corinthians 8:9) and of every believer who has nothing to bring.

settings.what: A short cry for quick help
settings.by: A poor and needy singer; the title names David
settings.to: God
settings.when: No occasion is given. The title "to bring to remembrance" may tie it to an offering ritual
settings.why: To give a short form of prayer for urgent need, taken from or parallel to 40:13–17, and to lead into Psalm 71.
settings.readers: Later Israel, who could pray it in any sudden trouble, as Christians and Jews have done since.

title: Do Not Leave Me When I Am Old
sum: Psalm 71 is the prayer of an old man who has trusted God since he was born. It begins with lines close to 31:1–3 and leans on God as a rock to live in. Enemies say God has abandoned him, and he asks God not to throw him away now that his hair is white and his strength is gone, until he can tell the next generation of God's mighty deeds. He looks back on many troubles and forward to God bringing him up again "out of the deep places of the earth", and he promises to sing to the Holy One of Israel on harp and lyre.

It has no title in the Hebrew, which leads many to read it with Psalm 70. The Greek gives it a title naming David, the sons of Jonadab and the first exiles. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 70.

views.H: Because it has no title and continues Psalm 70, traditional readers take it as David's prayer in old age, perhaps during Absalom's revolt or the plot of Adonijah (1 Kings 1). The Greek title links it with the Rechabites, the sons of Jonadab (Jeremiah 35), and the first exiles.
views.C: Scholars call it an individual lament woven from phrases of other psalms (22, 31, 35, 40), the work of a well-read temple singer. Its theme of old age and of God's care from birth is unusual in the Psalter. In 4QPs-a, Psalm 71 follows Psalm 38 directly, showing that the order of these psalms was not yet fixed.
views.L: The opening, "I take shelter in you, LORD; never let me end up in shame", closes the Te Deum ("in you, Lord, have I trusted; let me never be confounded"). Psalm 71 is a common psalm in prayers with the elderly and the dying.
views.J: Rashi reads the psalm as Israel's prayer in exile, which has trusted God since its birth as a nation at the Exodus.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in 71:20 a hope of resurrection, and Augustine read the whole psalm as the church, old in the world, still praising. Calvin stressed that the faith of one's youth must be renewed in old age.

settings.what: A lament and song of trust in old age
settings.by: An old man with enemies; no title in the Hebrew (the Greek names David)
settings.to: God
settings.when: No occasion is given. Traditional readers: David in old age. Scholars: an aged worshiper or temple singer, perhaps after the exile
settings.why: To ask God not to abandon a lifelong believer in weakness, and to hand down the story of God's deeds to the next generation.
settings.readers: Later Israel: The old among them had lived through ruin and return, and the psalm gave them words to pass on their faith.

title: Give the King Your Justice
sum: Psalm 72 is a prayer for the king. It asks God to give the king his justice, so that the king will defend the poor, save the children of the needy and break the oppressor. The prayer grows from justice to blessing: rain on the fields, peace until the moon is no more, rule from sea to sea, and kings from Tarshish, Sheba and Seba bringing gifts. Its reason is stated in the middle: the king will rescue the needy who have no helper, and "their blood will be precious in his eyes". It ends with the hope that all nations will bless themselves by him, echoing God's promise to Abraham.

The title reads "Of Solomon". After the psalm come the doxology that closes Book II (72:18–19) and the note "Here end the prayers of David son of Jesse" (72:20). In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 71.
readings: Read as a prayer for the king of Judah

The psalm was a prayer for a new king, perhaps at his crowning, setting out what a good king must be: a defender of the poor. Its high hopes (sea to sea, as long as the sun) are the language of royal courts in the ancient world, here bound to justice.
Read as a prayer for Solomon
The title and the details (Sheba, gold, wide rule, wisdom in judging) fit Solomon, and many readers take it as David's prayer for his son, or as Solomon's prayer for himself (1 Kings 3:9).
Read as a prayer for the Messiah
Already in the Targum, 72:1 is a prayer for "King Messiah", and the Talmud takes 72:17 as naming the Messiah. Christians read it as the reign of Christ, before whom the kings of the earth bow.
Read as a standard for every ruler
Many modern readers take the psalm as a measure of any government: power is legitimate when it protects the poor and needy and stops oppression.

views.H: The title "Of Solomon" can mean "by" or "for" Solomon. Readers who take it as "for" connect it with David's last days and Solomon's crowning (1 Kings 1:32–40; 1 Chronicles 29:22–23), which also explains 72:20: these were David's last prayers. The kingdom from the river to the sea (1 Kings 4:21, 24) and the gifts of Sheba (1 Kings 10:1–10) fit Solomon's reign.
views.C: Most scholars see a coronation psalm or a prayer for the king at a yearly festival, from the time of the kings of Judah. Its wording is close to Assyrian royal prayers and coronation hymns, but the stress on the poor sets it apart. The colophon of 72:20 shows that an earlier collection of David's prayers ended here; more psalms of David were added later (86, 101, 103, 108–110, 138–145).
views.L: In the Western church Psalm 72 is the psalm of the Epiphany, because of the kings who bring gifts (Matthew 2:11; Isaiah 60:6). Isaac Watts paraphrased it as "Jesus shall reign where'er the sun", and James Montgomery as "Hail to the Lord's Anointed".
views.J: The Targum renders 72:1 as "Give the laws of your justice to King Messiah". The Talmud says the Messiah's name is Yinnon, reading the verb of 72:17 as a name (Sanhedrin 98b), and lists his name among the things that existed before the world, from the same verse (Pesahim 54a). Rashi reads the psalm as David's prayer for Solomon, and Radak applies it also to the Messiah.
views.X: Christians read Psalm 72 as the reign of Christ, the son of David, whose kingdom spreads to all nations. The church fathers saw its fulfillment in the Magi. Many Christians, especially in liberation and Catholic social teaching, have also read it as God's standard for rulers in this world: judging the king by how he treats the poor.

echoes: 1 Kings 3:9–12; 1 Kings 4:21–25; 1 Kings 10:1–10; 2 Samuel 23:3–4; Genesis 12:3; Genesis 22:18; Isaiah 11:1–5; Isaiah 60:6; Zechariah 9:10; Matthew 2:11; 2:8; 89:36–37; 41:13; 106:48

settings.what: A prayer for the king, perhaps at his crowning
settings.by: A temple singer or the congregation; the title names Solomon
settings.to: God, about the king
settings.when: The title: Solomon. Scholars: a coronation or a royal festival in Judah
settings.why: To ask God to give the king justice, so that the poor are defended and the land and nations are blessed. It sets out what a king of David's line is for.
settings.readers: Later Israel: With no king on the throne, they prayed it for the son of David they hoped for, and so it became a prayer for the Messiah.
views: David's prayer for his son, or a prayer at Solomon's crowning.
A coronation prayer used for each new king.
After the exile, a hope for the coming king (Targum; New Testament).

settings.what: The doxology that closes Book II and the colophon
settings.by: The editors of the Psalter
settings.to: The congregation, which answers "Amen and amen"
settings.when: When the books of the Psalter were collected, probably after the exile
settings.why: To close the second book of the Psalms with blessing, as 41:13 closes the first, and to mark the end of a collection of David's prayers.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, who knew the Psalter in its five books, like the five books of Moses.

traditions.q: "May he rule from sea to sea" (72:8). When and how does the reign of Psalm 72 come?
views: The psalm describes Christ's future thousand-year reign on earth from Jerusalem, after his return, when all nations will literally serve him.

Christ already reigns, and the psalm is being fulfilled as the gospel spreads to the nations. Many Reformed writers expected that spread to fill the earth before his return, as in Isaac Watts' paraphrase; others hold that the full reign comes only at the new creation.
The kingdom of Christ is already present in the church as a seed and beginning, and will be completed at his return; the psalm is prayed for that kingdom at Epiphany.
The kingdom is already present in the church's worship, where heaven and earth meet, and will be revealed in full at Christ's coming; there is no earthly thousand-year reign.

deep.h: The king in Jewish and Christian reading
deep.b:
In its first setting the psalm is a prayer for a living king. It uses the high language of ancient royal courts: he should live as long as the sun and rule to the ends of the earth. What sets it apart is that its reason for all this blessing is the king's care for the poor (72:12–14).

In Jewish reading, the Targum turns the first line into a prayer for "King Messiah", and the Talmud finds the Messiah's name in 72:17. Medieval commentators held two readings together: Rashi read it as David's prayer for Solomon, and others, such as Radak, also as a hope for the king to come. Jewish interpreters note that the psalm describes justice and peace on earth, and they answer the Christian reading by asking where that peace is to be seen.

In Christian reading, the New Testament never quotes Psalm 72 directly, but the Magi bringing gold and frankincense (Matthew 2:11) echo 72:10–15 and Isaiah 60:6, and the church has read the psalm of Jesus since the early centuries. Christians answer the Jewish question in different ways: some say the reign has begun and is spreading, some that it will come with Christ's return, and some that both are true (see the traditions card).

Both traditions agree on the measure the psalm sets: a true king of David's line is known by what he does for the needy.

Each of the five books of the Psalms ends with a blessing (41:13; 72:18–19; 89:52; 106:48; with Psalm 150 closing the whole). This one is the fullest: it blesses the God who alone does wonders and prays that his glory will fill all the earth, echoing Numbers 14:21 and Isaiah 6:3.

Then comes a note found nowhere else in the Psalter: "Here end the prayers of David son of Jesse". It cannot mean that David wrote no other psalms, for Psalms 86, 101, 103, 108–110, 122, 124, 131, 133 and 138–145 carry his name. Most scholars take it as the ending of an older collection of David's psalms (roughly 3–41 and 51–72), kept when the larger Psalter was put together. Some note that 72:20, placed after a psalm for Solomon, makes the passing of the crown from David to his son the end of David's prayers.
